title: Munich air disaster
summary: British European Airways Flight 609, an Airspeed Ambassador en route from Belgrade to Manchester, stopped at Munich to refuel. After two aborted takeoff attempts due to engine boost surging, the crew attempted a third takeoff in snow and slush. The aircraft failed to become airborne, struck a fence at runway end, and the left wing was torn off when it struck a house beyond the runway. Altogether 23 died and 21 survived.
probable_cause: engine boost surging complications during takeoff, coupled with snow and slush on the runway affecting aircraft performance

factors.evidence: pilots abandoned two takeoffs because of boost surging in the left engine
snow was falling, causing a layer of slush to form at the end of the runway
an investigation originally blamed Thain, saying he did not de-ice the aircraft's wings
the left wing was ripped off when it struck a house

events.text: Rayment abandoned the take-off after Thain noticed the port boost pressure gauge fluctuating
A second attempt was made but called off 40 seconds into the attempt because the engines were running on an overrich mixture
It had started to snow heavily, and snow was falling, causing a layer of slush to form at the end of the runway
Thain told the station engineer that the only option was to hold the plane overnight but rejected this in favor of the third takeoff
The aircraft ploughed through a fence beyond the end of the runway and the left wing was ripped off when it struck a house

notes: Detailed sequence of takeoff attempts documented

title: United Airlines 736

location.name: Southwest of Las Vegas, Clark County, Nevada

summary: United Air Lines Flight 736, a Douglas DC-7 with 47 passengers and crew aboard, was flying at 21,000 feet over Clark County, Nevada, on April 21, 1958, when it collided in midair with a United States Air Force F-100F Super Sabre fighter jet crewed by two pilots. Both aircraft fell out of control and crashed into unpopulated desert terrain southwest of Las Vegas, leaving no survivors. The collision occurred in clear weather at high altitude with high closure speeds. The investigation determined that structural supports on both aircraft's canopies limited pilot visibility and contributed to the inability to see the other aircraft until too late.
probable_cause: The high rate of near head-on closure and cockpit visibility limitations. A metal frame support on the F-100's canopy interfered with the Air Force instructor pilot's ability to see the oncoming DC-7, while a supporting pillar on the DC-7's windshield could have prevented the United Airlines captain from sighting the fighter until too late.

factors.evidence: The DC-7 airliner collided with the F-100F Super Sabre fighter jet at 21,000 feet.
ATC authorities at CAA and Nellis Air Force Base failed to reduce known collision risks and failed to coordinate traffic separation for training exercises.
A metal frame support on the F-100's canopy interfered with the Air Force instructor pilot's ability to see the oncoming DC-7.
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year.

events.text: United 736 departed Los Angeles International Airport at 07:37 on a transcontinental flight to New York City.
F-100F Super Sabre took off from Nellis Air Force Base at 07:45 on a training flight with instructor in front seat and trainee under hood in rear seat.
United 736 merged onto Victor 8 airway at authorized cruise altitude of 21,000 feet en route to Denver.
DC-7 and F-100F collided head-on at 21,000 feet near Las Vegas with high closure speed; both aircraft lost control and crashed into desert terrain.

title: Aeroméxico 111
summary: An Aeroméxico Lockheed Constellation with experienced pilots departed Guadalajara at night during heavy rain on an instrument climb. The aircraft drifted from the correct course and began flying in a southwesterly direction toward Cerro Latillas mountain. The crew lost situational awareness without visual references and did not correct the navigation error. The aircraft crashed into the mountain killing all 45 occupants.
probable_cause: Spatial disorientation and loss of situational awareness due to instrument flight in poor weather and improper instrument-based navigation following takeoff.

factors.evidence: heavy rain late at night
the plane was flying low and was headed into an out-of-course path
the plane kept flying straight in a south-westerly direction
Spatial disorientation and loss of situational awareness were noted by investigators
Contact with ATC was severed after no update was received and another aircraft saw a fireball coming from the ground.

events.text: Aircraft took off from Runway 28 at Guadalajara at 21:53 CST in heavy rain with night conditions
Crew halted required left turn and set aircraft to straight direction, flying southwesterly instead of climbing toward Mexico City
Contact with ATC severed as aircraft continued flying off-course path at low altitude toward mountain
Aircraft crashed into Cerro Latillas mountain

notes: exact crash location inferred from narrative

title: KLM 607-E
summary: KLM Flight 607-E, a Lockheed Super Constellation named Hugo de Groot on the second leg of a transatlantic trip from Amsterdam to New York, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean after departing Shannon Airport, Ireland, on 14 August 1958. Radio contact was lost about 35 minutes after takeoff, and a rescue operation later found light debris and recovered the remains of 34 of the 99 people aboard roughly 180 km northwest of Shannon. Irish and Dutch investigators could not pinpoint a definitive cause but believed the most likely explanation was an over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing an oil feed line regulator valve, which may have provoked a flight disturbance and caused the propeller to shear off.
probable_cause: Investigators could not determine a definitive cause but considered the most likely explanation to be a malfunctioning over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing oil feed line regulator valves, which may have provoked a flight disturbance and caused the propeller to shear off.

factors.evidence: a malfunctioning over-speeding outboard propeller caused by metal particles obstructing oil feed line regulator valves
The particles may have been formed by a gear that was damaged when the supercharger of the corresponding engine was accelerated
The malfunctions of the propeller pitch might have provoked a flight disturbance and as a consequence the propeller may have sheared off

events.text: Flight 607-E departed Shannon Airport at 03:05 UTC on the second leg of a transatlantic trip from Amsterdam to New York City, with stops in Shannon and Gander.
Radio contact with the aircraft was lost at approximately 03:40 UTC.
The investigating board believed a malfunctioning over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing oil feed line regulator valves, provoked a flight disturbance.
The propeller may have sheared off, and a rescue operation later found light debris on the ocean surface about 180 km northwest of Shannon.

notes: Cause never conclusively determined; investigators only reached a probable hypothesis after considering bomb, electrical failure and pilot error.
Flight phase at time of loss of contact is not stated in the text.

title: Aeroflot 4
summary: The Tu-104A departed Khabarovsk and climbed to avoid towering cumulus clouds, reaching 12,000 m despite this being unsafe at the aircraft's takeoff weight of 66 tons. The aircraft encountered intense cumulonimbus clouds with strong updrafts that caused the aircraft to stall. Both engines flamed out during the stall, and the artificial horizons failed, rendering recovery nearly impossible.
probable_cause: The aircraft was flown to an unsafe altitude given its weight and encountered severe updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds, resulting in an aerodynamic stall. Insufficient analysis of weather conditions and lack of stall recovery procedures contributed to the accident.

factors.evidence: The aircraft climbed to 12000 m while weighted at 66 tons; altitudes of 12000 m could only be safely achieved in calm weather, and the weight limited maximum safe altitude to 11700 m at standard engine power.
Cumulonimbus clouds reaching altitudes of over 12000 m with strong updrafts between 11000 and the reported presence of strong updrafts within cumulonimbus clouds.
There were no defined procedures in place in the event of a stall, indicating lack of crew training for this situation.
The Tu-104 was prone to losing longitudinal stability in certain atmospheric conditions, could be followed by engine failure and artificial horizon failure.
The aircraft stalled, during which the engines flamed out and the landing gear was extended.
The aircraft crashed into a dense forest 215 km northwest of Khabarovsk airport, impacting the ground at an angle of 60°.

events.text: Flight 04 instructed to maintain flight at an altitude of 9000 m.
Crew requested permission to climb to 12000 m to avoid cumulus clouds and captain reported reaching 12000 m, stating they saw intense cumulus clouds ahead.
At 22:18 controller contacted Flight 4; an agitated voice only replied 'one minute, one minute' before the aircraft stopped responding to any later calls.
Between 22:20 and 22:25 the aircraft crashed into a dense forest 215 km northwest of Khabarovsk airport, impacting at an angle of 60° with a 450 m wide debris field.

title: 1958 Aeroflot Tu-104 crash in Chuvash
summary: Aeroflot Flight CCCP-42362, a Tupolev Tu-104A, was diverted from Moscow-Vnukovo due to heavy fog and proceeded to higher altitudes when flying into strong turbulence. The aircraft reached 12,000 meters altitude before entering a sharp, near-vertical dive and spin. The crew was unable to overcome the control forces and the aircraft crashed near Kanash. The investigation determined the crash was caused by loss of control from flying into strong turbulence causing the aircraft to exceed critical angles of attack.
probable_cause: Loss of control as a result of the aircraft flying into an area of strong turbulence which caused it to exceed critical angles of attack at high altitude.

factors.evidence: heavy fog caused authorization to land at Moscow-Vnukovo Airport to be denied by controllers
weather in Gorky was also deemed unsuitable for landing
suddenly flew into an area of high turbulence causing the aircraft to experience a sudden and drastic increase in pitch
force on the aircraft's horizontal stabilizers was too great for the pilots to overcome
aircraft entered a sharp, near vertical dive followed by a spin
Tu-104A crashed near Apnerka rail station, west of the town of Kanash

events.text: CCCP-42362 took off from Beijing en route to Moscow on 17 October 1958.
Authorization to land at Moscow-Vnukovo Airport was denied by controllers due to heavy fog.
The aircraft diverted to their alternate, Gorky Airport, before proceeding to Sverdlovsk after the weather was deemed unsuitable for landing there.
The aircraft was flying at an altitude of 10,000 meters when it suddenly flew into an area of high turbulence.
Caught in a powerful updraft, the aircraft abruptly reached an altitude of 12,000 meters and was standing on its hind legs.
The aircraft entered a sharp, near vertical dive followed by a spin from which the pilots could not recover.
The Tu-104A crashed near Apnerka rail station, west of the town of Kanash.
